title: Panelboards, Breakers and Panel Schedules

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Training room with a lighting panelboard; panel de-energized, lock and tag on the upstream disconnect, lead tech in PPE. Matthew narrates; medium shot.
scenes.says: Removing a dead front exposes energized parts unless the panel is dead. So the top control is de-energize, lock out and verify, which is what we've done here. If it can't be de-energized, it's energized work needing a risk assessment, PPE and a qualified person. Plan ahead: who's qualified, where the upstream lockout point is, and what else goes dark when you shut it off.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: On-screen safety callout over the panel door.
scenes.on_screen: Dead front off = energized-work exposure. Our company: only under an electrician's supervision.
scenes.says: Opening the door to operate a breaker is normal work. Removing the dead front exposes energized parts, and that's energized work requiring an arc-flash and shock risk assessment, PPE per the label or company table, and a qualified person. At our company, a tech working under an electrician's supervision may remove a dead front and swap a breaker, with the panel locked out whenever feasible. That's our company's stance; other companies may be stricter, so follow your company's written policy.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Lead tech removes the dead front of the locked-out panel; camera pushes in as each part is pointed out.
scenes.on_screen: Main lugs/main breaker | Bus A-B-C | Neutral bar | Ground bar | Dead front | Door | Nameplate
scenes.says: Here's the anatomy. The main lugs or main breaker, where the feeder lands; a main-lug-only panel is protected upstream. Bus bars carrying phases A, B and C, where breakers clip or bolt on. The neutral bar for grounded conductors, isolated from the enclosure in subpanels. The ground bar, bonded to the enclosure. The dead front. The door, with the directory. And the nameplate: voltage, phase, bus and short-circuit rating.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close-up: single-pole, two-pole and three-pole breakers; handle ties; SWD marking.
scenes.says: Breakers. Single-pole for 120 or 277 volt circuits. Two-pole for 208, 240 or 480 volt loads. Three-pole for three-phase loads. Handle ties join single-poles so multiwire circuit hots disconnect together. Breakers used as regular switches must be SWD marked for fluorescent, or HID marked for HID. And only install breakers listed or classified for that panel. A fits-in breaker may not contact the bus properly and can overheat.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close-up: three single-pole breakers feeding circuits that share a neutral, no handle tie. Red callout.
scenes.on_screen: Shared neutral without handle ties? Report it.
scenes.says: Multiwire branch circuits use two or three hots sharing one neutral, like circuits 1, 3 and 5. The NEC requires a way to disconnect all the hots together: a multi-pole breaker or listed handle ties. See single-poles sharing a neutral without ties? Report it. Opening that shared neutral with any of the circuits on is a serious shock hazard.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Typed panel schedule on a clipboard; on-screen highlights on '20/1', phase column and spares.
scenes.on_screen: Odd left, even right | 20/1 = 20 A 1-pole | Phases rotate A-B-C
scenes.says: Reading a panel schedule. Odd circuits on the left, even on the right. 20 slash 1 means 20 amps, one pole; 30 slash 2 means 30 amps, two pole, taking two positions. The phase column rotates A, B, C. Phase totals show balance; an unbalanced panel increases neutral current and voltage drop. Every circuit, spares included, needs its specific purpose. Lights isn't specific. Lighting, Warehouse Aisles 1 to 4 is.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Lead tech compares the typed schedule with installed breakers and marks corrections in ink.
scenes.says: Now compare the schedule with what's actually installed. Directories are wrong often, so never trust them alone. Before shutting a breaker off, confirm what else is on it; Corridor East might also feed emergency fixtures. Confirm with a tracer and live-dead-live. Found an error? Fix it neatly in ink or with a label maker, and note it on the work order. The next tech's safety depends on it.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Panel with door open and dead front on; inspection checklist on screen.
scenes.on_screen: Label | Directory | No open slots | No heat signs | Working space | Warm/tripping → report
scenes.says: With the door open and the dead front on, here's your basic inspection. Label legible and voltage identified. Directory present and plausible. No missing knockouts or open positions without filler plates. No signs of heat: discoloration, melted handles, burnt smell, buzzing. Working space clear. Any breaker warm through its handle, or tripping repeatedly? Report it. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: Panel de-energized and locked out, per the lesson's video suggestion; lead tech is a qualified person in PPE. Show the lock at the upstream disconnect and live-dead-live before the dead front comes off. Resolved (owner decision, November 2026): at our company a tech working under an electrician's supervision may remove a dead front and swap a breaker; this is a company stance that licensees must set for themselves, so re-record scene 2 if their policy differs. Techs still may not operate main breakers or switchgear (often the upstream lockout point); an electrician operates the upstream lockout.
